book_title: Skating Wild on an Inland Sea
subject_line: Two skaters on a frozen Lake Superior bay
email_body:
Dear Jean,

Skating Wild on an Inland Sea sends two children out early one morning onto a remote frozen bay of Lake Superior, and it reads like a book that could only come from someone who knows that shoreline from Thunder Bay. I would love to ask how much of that morning on the ice comes from your own winters, and how you and Todd Stewart worked out the balance of words and space.

book_title: The Dialogues: The Song of Francis Pegahmagabow
subject_line: Francis Pegahmagabow and the shape of The Dialogues
email_body:
Dear Armand,

The Dialogues follows Francis Pegahmagabow from home through the First World War and on to the making of the opera Sounding Thunder, moving between poems and lyric essays. That it won the Betsy Warland Between Genres Award seems fitting. I would be curious to hear why this life asked for a hybrid form, and how working alongside the opera shaped the book.

subject_line: Good medicine and dating in nedi nezu
email_body:
Dear Tenille,

I'm curious how the Dene word in the title shaped the way you thought about the poems as a whole, and whether your photography ever feeds the way you build a poem.

book_title: All the Little Monsters: How I Learned to Live with Anxiety
subject_line: Writing All the Little Monsters after 33 books
email_body:
Dear David,

After more than thirty books, your new memoir All the Little Monsters turns to your own experience of living with anxiety. It came out the same year you took on the editorial director role at Swift Water Books. I'd like to ask what changed in your writing when the subject became your own mind rather than a character's, and whether editing other Indigenous writers has altered how you approach your own drafts.

book_title: Superfan: How Pop Culture Broke My Heart
subject_line: Anne of Green Gables and grief in Superfan
email_body:
Dear Jen,

I was struck by how Superfan uses pop culture as a lens on family and grief, especially the essay linking your childhood attachment to Anne of Green Gables and Matthew Cuthbert's death to losing your father when you were twelve. I'd like to ask how you decided which cultural touchstones could carry that much weight, and how writing the memoir in pieces sits alongside your newer novel, The Hunger We Pass Down.

subject_line: Niobe and the language of loss in Shadow Blight
email_body:
Dear Annick,

In your Writers' Federation of Nova Scotia spotlight, you explained that you turned to the myth of Niobe in Shadow Blight because you had struggled to find language for your own miscarriages that felt right. The book went on to win the Governor General's Award for Poetry. I'd like to ask how you decided where the myth should lead and where the contemporary voice should take over.

book_title: The Greatest Hits of Wanda Jaynes
subject_line: From a grocery store to Taking Down Names
email_body:
Dear Bridget,

I read in a CBC piece how everyday grocery shopping worked its way into The Greatest Hits of Wanda Jaynes, a novel that turns on a shooting in a grocery store and was later adapted into a film. Your newer novel, Taking Down Names, follows a journalist in Newfoundland and Labrador investigating deaths tied to online wrongdoing. I'd like to ask what draws you to ordinary places and habits as the starting point for darker stories.

book_title: Epekwitk: Mi'kmaq Poetry from Prince Edward Island
subject_line: Pairing poems and your own artwork in Epekwitk
email_body:
Dear Julie,

In Epekwitk: Mi'kmaq Poetry from Prince Edward Island, each poem sits beside artwork you made yourself, like one voice in two forms. As PEI's first Indigenous Poet Laureate, and co-author of Amazing L'nu'k with Robin Grant, you have spent a lot of time sharing Mi'kmaw stories with readers of every age. Do the images or the words usually come first for you?

subject_line: Living with The Leopard while writing Lampedusa
email_body:
Dear Steven,

You've said you first came across The Leopard in your early twenties and have reread it many times since, and that long companionship seems to sit underneath Lampedusa, your novel of Giuseppe Tomasi di Lampedusa's final years and the manuscript he never saw published. I'd like to ask how you balanced your own long reading of the book against the need to imagine its author from the inside, and whether your poetry shaped the novel's sentences.
